milestones.label: The American Federation of Teachers declines to oppose corporal punishment
milestones.claim: The American Federation of Teachers has no resolution opposing school corporal punishment; its only resolution on the subject (1976) intervened in Ingraham v. Wright to protect 'a teacher's right to maintain discipline in the classroom,' though the AFT endorsed the federal Protecting Our Students in Schools Act in 2023.

milestones.label: The Supreme Court rules school corporal punishment is not cruel and unusual punishment
milestones.claim: In Ingraham v. Wright (1977), a 5-4 Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment does not apply to corporal punishment in public schools and that due process does not require a hearing before paddling because state tort and criminal remedies suffice; it expressly left open whether excessive corporal punishment violates substantive due process.

milestones.label: The National PTA calls for an end to corporal punishment in schools
milestones.claim: National PTA's position statement says it will support efforts to abolish corporal punishment and to develop alternative discipline programs.

milestones.label: New Mexico becomes the 31st state to prohibit it
milestones.claim: New Mexico prohibited corporal punishment in schools through HB 172, signed by Republican Governor Susana Martinez on April 6, 2011 after passing the House 36-31 and the Senate 22-17.

milestones.label: The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry opposes it
milestones.claim: The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry's 2012 policy statement does not support corporal punishment as a method of behavior modification and urges its members to advise school boards accordingly.

milestones.label: A coalition of national organizations writes to every governor and chief state school officer
milestones.claim: In November 2016 more than 100 organizations, including the ACLU, APA, AFT, NEA, AAP, NAACP, SPLC and the Children's Defense Fund, signed an open letter organized by the National Women's Law Center calling for an end to corporal punishment in schools.

milestones.label: The last district in North Carolina stops, ending the practice statewide without a law
milestones.claim: All 115 North Carolina school districts had prohibited corporal punishment by October 2, 2018, when Graham County became the last to vote to end it, although state law (G.S. 115C-390.4) still permits it.

milestones.label: The American Academy of Pediatrics calls for abolition
milestones.claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2018 policy statement on discipline concludes that aversive strategies including all forms of corporal punishment are minimally effective in the short term and not effective in the long term.

milestones.label: The American Psychological Association adopts its resolution
milestones.claim: The American Psychological Association adopted a resolution in February 2019 opposing physical discipline of children by parents, citing the 2016 meta-analysis; it does not address school corporal punishment directly.

milestones.label: The National Association of School Psychologists takes its position
milestones.claim: The National Association of School Psychologists 'strongly opposes the use of corporal punishment in schools and supports ending its use in all schools' (position statement, revised 2021).

milestones.label: Colorado prohibits it
milestones.claim: Colorado prohibited corporal punishment in public schools and licensed child care on April 20, 2023 through HB23-1191, which passed the House 48-16 and the Senate 32-0.

milestones.label: Idaho prohibits it
milestones.claim: Idaho banned corporal punishment and chemical restraint in public and charter schools on April 3, 2023 through House Bill 281, a restraint-and-seclusion bill carried by a Republican sponsor; it passed the House 45-22 and the Senate 21-12.

milestones.label: Kentucky reaches zero without a statewide ban
milestones.claim: Kentucky recorded zero instances of corporal punishment in the 2023-24 school year after all 171 school districts adopted prohibiting policies by November 2, 2023, driven by a state board regulation rather than a statute.

milestones.label: A federal circuit split opens over whether students can sue
milestones.claim: Seven federal circuits allow a student to sue over excessive corporal punishment under substantive due process ('shocks the conscience'), two under the Fourth Amendment, and the Fifth Circuit alone, covering Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, denies any federal claim where state remedies exist; the Supreme Court has declined to review that rule five times, most recently in January 2024.

milestones.label: The Protecting Our Students in Schools Act is reintroduced in Congress
milestones.claim: The Protecting Our Students in Schools Act, which would bar corporal punishment in any school receiving federal funds, was introduced as H.R. 3265 on May 8, 2025 with 21 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee; no version since 2010 has had a hearing or markup, and as of September 2026 no Senate companion has been introduced in the 119th Congress despite press releases saying one would be.

milestones.label: Oklahoma prohibits it for students with disabilities
milestones.claim: Oklahoma's SB 364, prohibiting corporal punishment of students with disabilities, became law in May 2025 without Governor Kevin Stitt's signature after passing the Senate 31-16 and the House 63-25.

milestones.label: Florida narrows it
milestones.claim: Since July 1, 2025, Florida districts that allow corporal punishment must obtain parental consent, either for the school year or before each instance, under HB 1255 (the statute says 'consent,' not 'written consent'; the second-adult and written-explanation rules predate it in § 1003.32), which passed both chambers unanimously on final votes and was signed May 30, 2025.

note: State years are the year the state prohibited corporal punishment in public schools. District dates are the date printed on that district's own policy, which is usually the date it was last revised. Districts prohibiting with no date on the policy are counted but not placed in time.
